blocks.x: Bonafide Jazz Bands

I couldn't say that with authority. I could say that they played jazz, but to say they were not Bonafide Jazz Bands would call for definitions which I'm not competent to give or I'm not even competent to identify. You know what I mean? I'm just not that conversant with the whole jazz movement. It was something which I'd say sort of passed me by without my being opposed to it, without my being any part of it. So jazz has actually meant absolutely nothing in my life, in my musical experience. It's meant nothing to me. On the other hand, I have never felt that it offended me. See what I mean? Now, by, by, by, well you can pull your hair out over the screeches of Mr. Presley in that rocker school of, of, uh, so-called entertainment. Uh, uh, heck I like, you know, at the ballpark for example, the old days, the baseball park. I remember going back in 1926, 27, and then every Sunday at the Doubleheader they'd have a band in the Negro Bleachers. And they'd play that, uh, Maryland Roll-Class . call the court, da da da da da da da da da da da da da da da da da da da. And man, the crowd would go crazy. The white people they would really like to do. Sure, everybody would love it. Every time the Pelicans were on a rally or the Pelicans come to bat they'd give a couple of these fan fairs and go off into it. That used to be a regular feature on some of those when you have eight and ten, that's when baseball would do eight and ten, twelve thousand people on a Sunday. When was that, during the 20s? You were in the great days of the 20s, yeah, I'd say from 23 to 20, maybe 23 to 30, somewhere in that period.
Thank you. Well, getting back to the parties again, would you say that most of the musicians that played, maybe the poppers, they tend to play mostly jazz music?

Once again, you're trying to qualify me as an expert, of which I'm not. I don't expect it. I really don't know. What did you think of that? I would say it is hard to put your finger, or for me, who is not a student of jazz, to put my finger on a period at which what was once known as ragtime, when it was then considered to be jazz. Where the transition...
I'm not worried about the difference between jazz and ragtime, do they tend to play pop

music? They played what was hot for the day. They played jadda jadda, jing jing jing, pretty baby, pretty, that sort of stuff. But where 20 years earlier they were playing I Wonder Who's Kissing Her Now, which would be waltzy. The thing was pepped up and jazzed up as the expression went. The music was definitely jazzed up. I would say that was part of the evolution, yes.
Did you tend to have a lot of...

Once again, I can't ask you. I don't know... Did they tend to have a lot of colored bands? I would say without knowing, I would say that there was no... that there were considerable colored bands used.
What about... have Blanco such as debutante parties? Would they have a jazz band at a debutante party? I can't answer that question. Like I say, I wasn't a DD.

Alright, well, you say... You said there comes somebody who might be able to answer your question. Polly? Yeah. This is Mr. Hilliard, my brother-in-law, Mr. LeBuff, Mr. Hilliard. Now we're coming in and being a good for me. He said they do a full follow. Did they do a little bit like B4? No. Okay, more than I did.
Well, you said that jazz didn't offend you. Did you, you know, did a lot of people say

the thing, it was just rotten gutter, claptrap, claptrap? A lot of people did. And I wouldn't doubt for a moment that I went through a period in which I felt that. But I mean the overall feeling that I have now is that it didn't offend me and that it doesn't offend me. Although I would never go out and seek it. What about Alvin? Keep quiet. I never would go out and seek it as a form of entertainment. And when I, I've always under certain conditions, loved Papa Celestan for example. And when the saints go marching in or hear Susha and his group play, particularly Ed Marr singing that grapple-throated, if ever I cease to love version of the Mardi Gras. But that's the best answer I can give you. I just feel confident that if my memory is correct, there were times when I did look down my nose in jazz.
And you said a great number of people that did? I think there were, I think there were many that did. Would you say a majority of New Orleans?

No, I'd say the majority accepted it. I'd say the majority accepted it and recognized it as, well you see, here's the point. If a person was a dancer and a dance goer and a party man, and he'd hear it at the parties and hear it at the dances, he had to be part of his experience. I didn't go in for that much. And as a consequence, my experience was less limited than someone else's. And your liking or disliking for something is frequently predicated upon your experience. Yes, sir. So, not having had sufficient experience, you see what I mean?
Yes, sir. Well, taking all that for granted then, what did you, did you know an incisible amount of people who were greatly enthused over it?

I wouldn't say that I knew a great number that were enthused over it, but I would certainly say that those who enthused over it actually really enthused over it. You know what I mean? They were devotees. Yes, sir. They were devotees.
Well, uh... Among these, uh... people, uh... you said that most of the people that did like it were people who went to dance. Did I just think of it as a form of entertainment, just, uh, music?
No, no, no. You were asking me to project myself back 30 years into somebody's mind that I didn't, wasn't going to have been in a position to do then. I can't answer that, honestly.

Well, uh, put it this way. Did you, uh... Do you think, just in your opinion, which you, which of course you have qualified, think that, in fact, of it, that most people you knew that did like it tend to think of it just as something just to go and listen to, to have fun, and do they think of it as music of, of, with intrinsic values that classical music has?

I think their first impression must have been that it's something to have fun, to, to trip the light fantastic with, but that, uh, the final analysis gradually, this idea of it as an emerging art form, or an indigenous southern New Orleans art form, uh, uh, came about.
Well, uh, it won't matter, it'll come in, but not too, not too badly.
Uh, probably, tell you twice now a little bit.

Well, uh, could you, sort of, uh, carry it down to present day, did you, uh, have you noticed any increase in interest in jazz, or any time when people stop listening to it all, listen to it all together?
Or stop listening to it for a good deal? Oh no, I think, I think the interest is continuing. I think that...
Even during the 30s, would you say that?

I would say so. But I would say that jazz evolved, I think, you got to the point where you're going to... Well, I'm talking about, about, of course... The basic jazz? The basic jazz, rather than the derivation of such a swing. Well, you've had derivation, you've had swing, and you've had symphonic jazz, and you've had, uh, what? I'm talking about New Orleans jazz. New Orleans jazz. I, I would say, without knowing again, I would say that it's, uh, maintained a, uh, a, a vogue, uh, uh, what we have today they call Dixieland, is a, is a present day version of what was originally New Orleans, was it, isn't that correct? After fashion, yes. After fashion, see, I'm, I'm, I'm really, I'm really not, I'm dealing in some of the things I'm really not qualified to deal with, and all I can give you is a, a man on the other side of the fence, looking into the pasture, see? Less than a looking for. And, uh, I can't see all the animals in the pasture, because I'm not close enough to them, you don't know enough about the animal husbandry. That's the way it is with jazz.
Well, would you, you say there's been an increase in, and, do you think a lot of people now, today, think of it as music with, with intrinsic worth? I'm sure they do. I'm, I'm satisfied they do.
I'm satisfied.
The reality of New Orleanians, are your acquaintances, you would say, think of it as something?
I would say that many New Orleanians think so, yes, I would say so.
Do you know anybody in the present day who looks down at the camera and show music?

On the other hand, I've heard Orleanians say that there must be other ways in which $75,000 can be spent without, without writing the history of, of jazz in New Orleans. In other words, I, that's my reaction.
You know, I think that's a waste of time, right? I'm quite sure, there are many of my acquaintances who feel that. Do you feel that?

I don't feel any research project is a waste of time. I may not like the end result, but I don't think any project is a waste of time. I think if somebody spends $75,000 writing the history of sewerage in New Orleans, at some subsequent date, that's going to be an important body of material on the history of New Orleans. And therefore, anything, even though I'm not enthused about jazz per se, I'm not opposed to it, $75,000 spent in research on jazz, as far as I'm concerned, is a valuable contribution, because it's a contribution to the history of New Orleans. And as a person interested in history and in New Orleans, I think all facets of it are important, even though I may not be interested in that particular facet.
Well, you would say, though, that a lot of people do kind of think that's a waste of time and money.
I wouldn't be able to evaluate how many.
But you do know people of your acquaintance.
I've heard the expression made. I've heard the expression presented.
So you would say there are still diversions of opinions that you know of, any people still think of jazz as just got a clap track?

I'm quite sure there must be some. I've got a dear friend, for example, who's got a marvelous collection of operatic records. The gentleman just celebrated his 50th anniversary, his wedding anniversary, and he's got a marvelous collection of operatic records. I'm quite satisfied with jazz as today. It's an untouchable, just as it was 50 years ago, or 40 years ago, or 20 years ago.
In other words, today still there's a great divergence of opinion on it.
I'd say that there are divergences. How great? I would say the divergences are less great today than they were 30 years ago.
And then more people do appreciate it.
I'd say the proportion of those who have accepted it as an art form is greater today than it was 25 or 30 years ago. That's just a yes.

Do you think of anything you could add on this subject? I don't know what I've said on this subject. This is purely a search in the dark. Well, if you're sure it'll help. All right. Could you add the ages of your...
Ages of your... Yeah. My father was born in 1854 and died in 1913, which I think would make him 59 years old. My mother was born in 1865 and died in 1943, which would make her 78.
Oh, when she used to go to the opera, that was from...

It was prior to 1919 at the old French Opera House, because that's when the Opera House burned. And that would mean she went from her almost infancy back in the 70s, when everybody in the audience... But the one thing they did, they went to the Opera House, they lived in the Opera House, virtually. And the Opera House burned in 1919, if you know. And since then we've had opera, but not the opera that was the opera of 1840s down to 1919.

Thank you very much, sir. Okay, give me a name, please. My name is Lee Carroll. When were you born and where? I was born on October 11, 1938, in New Orleans. Have you lived in New Orleans all your life? No, I lived in Bay St. Louis, Mississippi, about 60 miles to New Orleans for seven years. From what age to what age would you say? From the age of... From the age of 10 to the age of 16. When did you first become aware of the intention of such a form of music as New Orleans jazz? Well, when I was about 12 years old, I heard for the first time, Pomp Selstein's band. And I believe it was the old Pestridge-Stand Yacht Club. Oh. What did you... What did you think of the music? Oh, I thought it was very good. I enjoyed it thoroughly. What about your fans? They all liked it, too. As a matter of fact, we used to make a point of going to all the dances that they had, to hear Pomp Selstein. What about your parents and your parents' friends? Do you know what they thought of it? Well, my parents, of course, had heard Dixieland ever since it first began back in the early 20s and everything. And they... I'd say they liked Dixieland. But I mean, they wouldn't go out of their way to hear it. But you would go out of their way to hear it. And you said your friends liked it, too? Yes, they all liked it. What did you think of? Do you think it was just something to... Music that you enjoyed listening to, to dance to, or do you think of it as an art form? Well, of course, for us, it was the only kind of music we would listen to. I don't know, at that age, I don't believe we ever really considered things as art forms. But that was all we wanted to listen to, certainly. And you said you first started listening to it in about 1950, you would say? Yes, 50 or 51. And how... Your group liked it, did they ever continue to like it, would you say? Which can you... Well, um... I myself liked Dixieland well enough. I progressed some progressive music more. And a lot of my friends have switched to liking, uh, what they call rock and roll them. More than Dixieland. Could you say about when they stopped liking New Orleans jazz design, liking rock and roll? I'd say about when... When rock and roll or rhythm and blues, it used to be, first came out about five years ago, in 1953. Well, uh, they... Uh... When they did like it from 50, 51, to 53, did they prefer jazz or popular music? Oh, yeah, of course. And... Do you know that many people now who really like jazz? Dixieland? Yeah. Yeah, I know quite a few people who like Dixieland. Uh... See, when I say they like, uh, rock and roll, I don't mean they have totally given up Dixieland or anything like that. They just prefer the, uh... Say, like, as if there were two dancers in a night. And one of them had a rock and roll band, the other had, say, Selstein. Well, I think most of them go to the dance that has a rock and roll band. Mm-hmm. But if there was one, if there was a dance with Selstein, they wouldn't have loved it. Uh, we'd say that the, the attitude most of the people that listen to New Orleans jazz now is, uh, that it's just something to dance to and have a good, accompany a good time, or, uh, what they think of it as, as great music. Yeah. And I think there's, some people think of classical music as great music. I think some people think of, uh, Dixieland, and when you say Dixieland, I take that you mean the, uh, New Orleans music. New Orleans jazz. I think some of them would, would listen to it as an art form, which is, I believe, what you, but, uh, I think the majority of them would just listen to it as good time music, just in more or less the same spirit as they'd listen to the rhythm and blues. Uh, do you think anything else to add on the subject of social accessibility of the jazz? Oh, uh, what, you, you said at dance, it may be, but, would you say that, uh, for the majority of social functions from, say 1950 to 1953, that would have, uh, New Orleans jazz bands if they could do it? Uh, certainly, everybody trying to get Selstein. He was, uh, in great demand. They haven't got anybody else? Or was it just Selstein or anything? Not that I know of. They didn't have Selstein, they just had, uh, a pop band, which nobody could stand. Yeah. And, uh, would, would you say, uh, nowadays they tend to high, like, low bands, rather than? Yes. I don't know, some people still do Selstein for the parties. Um, what about the debutant parties, you said, high bands, social functions, what, what, would you say, what, what have you noticed mostly? Well, I think they tend to, uh, get people on Selstein if they intend to have that kind of music. Do you think they, would they, would they, would they, would they, would they have more, uh, uh, New Orleans jazz, or, uh, uh, uh, uh, sweet band, or, you know, a, you know, a mid band played popular music, which is, they tend to get more. Yeah, I think they probably tend to get more. Yeah, I think they're probably trying to get more. Yeah. Do you think of anything else you can add, Selstein? No. No, not really, um. Well, thank you very much. Thank you. Okay, your name, please.
Clown, I'm a little bit.
Would you mind repeating that?
Clown, I'm a little bit.
How old are you? Thirteen. Uh, when were you born as well?
March 1st, New Orleans.
March 1st, what, nineteen?
Nineteen, forty-five.
Uh, what kind of music do you prefer to listen to? Rock and roll. Do you know, do you like New Orleans jazz?
Yeah.
But you prefer rock and roll. Rock and roll. Uh, what about your friends? What do you think they prefer to listen to?
Rock and roll.
Do a larger amount of them like jazz, second to rock and roll?
No, most of them like rock and roll.
Well, I mean, no I'm like jazz at all, would you say?
Oh, I like jazz.
Uh, but your, your, your friends. What about your friends? Yeah, they like jazz too.
But they prefer rock and roll. Uh, what about at parties you might go to?
What kind of bands do you tend to have mostly? Rock and roll bands. Some of them have South Stand bands. Some of them have South Stand bands. Some of them have South Stand bands.
Some of them have South Stand bands. But mostly rock and roll. Alright, thank you very much. Alright, your name please.

Abby Arnold. Uh, your date of birth and place for birth? September 25th, 1937 in Baptist Hospital New Orleans. Have you been to New Orleans all your life? Uh, when did you first come where there was such a folk music, New Orleans jazz? I think for as long as I can remember. Yeah, thank you very much. Thank you very much. Thank you very much. Thank you. Alright, your name please.
Abby Arnold.

dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear I was just all around me. Well when you first thought about it did you just like it? Well naturally

I always liked it because my father had a great deal to do with it and he played it more so than any other kind of music and so it just became more or less part of me. He played it you mean he played instruments or he played records? Both. He played the piano then he had other people in to play other instruments and then he he has a pretty good collection of it on records. What would you say your friends think of it? I think most of my friends. Well thought of it then I should say. Well thought of it then that was back around when I was. When you first started going after parties. When we first started going after parties it was it was just about the only form of music as far as my friends were concerned. That it was the only kind of band that we would consider getting for a good time and it was the only kind of music that we would go all the way down to the French Quarter to listen to.
Would you say most of the parties you went to then
about what age was this when you started going after? From between 14 to 17 high school years.
Would you say most of the parties they intended to have jazz bands? Definitely.

What bands would they have usually? Well they usually have cellist dance and then and then for serious dances like serrani dances every once in a while they would have pop bands which never were accepted with too much enthusiasm but it was just sort of the style that when you were going to have a serious dance you had to have semi-serious music.
In other words jazz wasn't thought to be socially high brown enough enough?
Not socially high brown enough but at times not in keeping with with long evening dresses and tuxedos but not that it carried any social stigma as far as acceptable music for parties went.
What did your parents and your parents contemporaries think about it?

Oh well they were strictly for jazz and nothing else as far as party music. There were only two kinds of music as far as they were concerned, classical music and jazz. Not your parents, what about your parents friends? Well most of my parents friends thought the same way. They've always been great jazz enthusiasts. All right. How old are your parents?
What about your parents? What about your parents?
My father's in his early 50s and my mother's in her late 40s.
Have you noticed that he changed his attitude towards jazz since when he first started going there since about age 14?
Do you mean among my contemporaries or my parents?
Not among your contemporaries? Yes. And with you too?
Yes, it's branched out into other forms of jazz, progressive jazz and all that. It's still considered one of the best forms of party music though.
That's what most of you think of being one of the best forms of party music? Yes. Have you ever thought of it as just as part of music or have you ever thought of it as a art form?

I thought of it as an art form only in its greatest musicians and I don't think that its greatest musicians are in New Orleans anymore. I think that Celestan's band for one can be considered one of the best jazz bands in the country but not as a, uh, not on a program that you would sit and listen to. I think you can hear the best jazz at a party because I think, I think that part of jazz is its reactions in its audience and that comes best at a party atmosphere rather than a concert atmosphere. But still I think that there are great jazz artists in the world that I would just sit and listen to rather than dance to.
That would be New Orleans jazz.
What do you mean New Orleans jazz?
I'm probably certain of New Orleans jazz.
As it is in New Orleans now or as it has originated in New Orleans?
New Orleans jazz is in New Orleans jazz, jazz tradition. As it is in New Orleans now also as it was in New Orleans.

Well if you're speaking of people like, like Louis Armstrong, Sidney Bichet and Kid Ory and those who I think they are some of the greatest jazz artists in the world and that they rate sitting and listening to either on records or in person. But I think that jazz as it is now in New Orleans has strictly become more a form of music to be enjoyed rather than to sit and listen to it seriously. For one thing the best artists get paid more out of New Orleans than they do in New Orleans.
Well, when you say jazz was the most popular form of music when you were in high school. What about college in New Orleans?
Well, I think washing roll was coming to the fore as party music. And I think it is now. Because it's earthier.
Well, if someone would say, that attitude was, you know, friends and, you know, parents and their friends and jazz is a social acceptable form of music.
Oh, definitely. I think that people still look forward to a party with jazz, much more than they would look forward to a party with any form of pop music.
But now they have a chance to prefer a lot more than when you and your friends?
Yes, because it makes for a wilder party. But if you add...
Which you prefer to listen to and go to dance and dance to? Which you prefer?

Well, it depends strictly on the mood and on the type of party. I think that a beer drinking rowdy party is best with a rock and roll band. I think a party with a great variety of people with a great variety of ages, all of them respond to jazz because it seems to be a much commoner medium than rock and roll is. And I think everyone will have fun at a party with New Orleans jazz, whereas only the strictly the younger people will have fun at a party with rock and roll. But if you're speaking of jazz as a serious form of listening to music, well, among the people who look at music at all consider it from a serious artistic standpoint, I think they definitely do consider jazz worthy to be listened to.
Most of the people, the majority of New Orleans people, you're according to it, have that idea, you think?
The ones who consider music seriously at all would, would enjoy sitting down and listening to a good jazz artist.
Do you think of anything else you could add on the topic of social acceptance of New Orleans jazz, by New Orleans, acceptance and acceptability?

Well, I think that the social acceptance of New Orleans jazz by New Orleans is strictly based upon New Orleans' love for a good time. And that jazz has always represented a good time. And it still represents a good time. And even though rock and roll, which is only a degenerate form of jazz, has come to the floor lately, it still can't replace jazz completely as good time music.
Anything else?

Well, it's a bit about listening to it seriously. I think that there are few people anyway in New Orleans among my siblings. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm.

I will sit down and give a lot of time to listening to music anyway, and I think among those who do, they will appreciate the fact that there are many jazz artists who are worth sitting down and listening to.
That's all. That's all. Thank you very much. Do I? This interview was recorded on Tuesday night, 13th of May, 1958.
